value: Study analyzed 6,874 publicly available metagenomes from 36 datasets across 6 continents and 25 countries
Reconstructed 1,023 high-quality P. copri genomes (17 isolate genomes, 1,006 metagenome-assembled genomes)
Identified four distinct P. copri clades (A, B, C, D) with inter-clade ANI distance >10%
Inter-clade ANI distances range from 13.0% to 21.4%
Four clades are >23% distant from other Prevotella, Alloprevotella, and Paraprevotella species
Core genome SNV distance between clades >10%
16S rRNA gene alone insufficient to distinguish clades
Ancient metagenomics analysis includes Iceman (5,300-year-old ice mummy) and pre-Columbian Mexican coprolites (1,300±100 BP)
P. copri clade diversification estimated to have begun ~6.5 million years ago (clade B split)
Clade A, D, C diversification estimated between ~3.5 and ~2.5 million years ago
Clade divergence occurred well before human migration out of Africa (420 ka minimum estimate vs 90-194 ka migration)
No strong evidence for disease associations at clade level across 10 disease datasets analyzed (CRC, T2D, hypertension, liver cirrhosis, IBD)
Distinct carbohydrate metabolism repertoires observed between clades
Clade B lacks β-galactosidase found in other clades
Clade B highly prevalent and nearly exclusive to pectin-degrading CAZy families PL9 and PL10
Clade D enriched in GH9 cellulase family
Multi-generational dietary modifications proposed as driver of P. copri underrepresentation in Westernized populations
uncurated_metadata.evidence_quote: In a cross-continent meta-analysis exploiting >6,500 metagenomes, we obtained >1,000 genomes and explored the genetic and population structure of P. copri.
uncurated_metadata.notes: Comprehensive metadata about study design, sample size, genomic characteristics, evolutionary history, and functional diversity of P. copri clades.

host_species.notes: Study focuses on human gut microbiome; host is implicitly human throughout the paper.

extraction_warnings: This paper is primarily a cross-continent meta-analysis with >6,500 metagenomes assembled into >1,000 P. copri genomes. Most samples are not individually described; sample-level metadata is sparse in the main text. Only cohorts newly sequenced in this work (Ghana, Tanzania, Ethiopia, Madagascar, and ancient samples) have sufficient detail for per-sample extraction. The schema fields were populated based on these newly sequenced datasets and available metadata.
Individual sample IDs are not provided in the paper for most participants. Sample identifiers are cohort-based or described generically (e.g., 'family samples').
For Ethiopia cohort: age of infants reported as average (1.31 years) with range; individual ages not provided.
For Ghana cohort: age of adults reported as average (33.14 years) and children as average (6.81 years); sex distribution reported as percentages, not per-sample.
For Tanzania cohort: age of adults reported as average (29.27 years) and children as average (8.22 years); sex distribution reported as percentages.
DNA extraction kit is listed as 'other' for ancient samples with protocol reference (chloroform-based extraction); specific commercial kit name not stated.

The paper reports sequencing on 'Illumina HiSeq2500 100nt paired end' for newly sequenced non-Westernized cohorts and 'Illumina HiSeqX 150-base pair paired-end' for some ancient samples; mapped to 'IlluminaHiSeq' enum.
Ancient sample dating: Iceman dated at ~5,300 years; coprolites radiocarbon dated to AD 673-768 (1,284 ± 16 BP) for sample 2180, approximate date 1,300 ± 100 BP for site.
No explicit age or sex reported for individual Ghana, Tanzania, or extended family samples; metadata reflect reported aggregates only.

Target_condition set to 'Healthy' for all newly sequenced cohorts as paper states 'All individuals sampled in this study were healthy defined as free of self-reported disease.' Disease cohorts (CRC, T2D, IBD, etc.) are from publicly available external datasets, not newly sequenced.
Body_site_details populated based on text descriptions; 'lower intestinal tract' for Iceman, 'coprolite (fossilized feces)' for Mexican samples.
Family relationship data provided only for Ethiopia (mother-infant pairs) and Ghana/Tanzania (extended families); individual family roles and IDs largely not reported.

Study is a cross-continent meta-analysis of metagenomes for P. copri population structure, not a clinical trial or disease study. Newly sequenced cohorts (Ghana, Ethiopia, Tanzania) comprised healthy individuals only.
Age data reported as group ranges and means, not per-sample; granularity set to subgroup_level by geographic cohort.
Most clinical metadata fields (BMI, disease details, medications, neonatal measures, OB-GYN parameters, smoking) are not reported in the paper.
Paper includes ancient metagenomes and analysis of disease associations from public datasets, but the newly sequenced participants had no reported disease or clinical conditions.
Batch 2 returned granularity='study_level', differs from batch 0 ('sample_level'); kept batch 0.

This is a microbial population genomics and metagenomics study, not a clinical trial or cohort study with individual patient outcomes. Most schema fields designed for clinical studies (ECOG, tumor size, OS) are not applicable.
No per-sample data provided in tabular format; paper reports aggregated statistics at study level and by population/lifestyle subgroup (Westernized vs non-Westernized).
Disease association analysis found no strong clade-level associations despite testing 10 disease phenotypes; this null result is important context.
Biomarker data is primarily microbiological (P. copri prevalence, clade composition, genetic distances, CAZyme families) rather than clinical lab values.
Ancient samples analyzed (Iceman, Mexican coprolites) but these are not modern human subjects with clinical data.
